title: HTTP: Methods, Status Codes & Headers
summary: **HTTP** is the request/response protocol of the web: methods (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) express intent, status codes report outcome, and headers carry metadata (content type, caching, auth, CORS). HTTPS adds encryption.

subtopics.title: Methods
subtopics.explanation: GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE removes. GET/HEAD are safe and idempotent; POST is not.

subtopics.title: Status codes
subtopics.explanation: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error (400/401/403/404), 5xx server error. Use the right one — clients branch on it.

subtopics.title: Headers
subtopics.explanation: Metadata: Content-Type, Cache-Control, Authorization, Set-Cookie, and the CORS Access-Control-* headers.

subtopics.title: HTTPS
subtopics.explanation: TLS encrypts the connection so traffic can't be read or tampered with; required for many browser APIs.

foundations.overview: HTTP is the protocol browsers and servers speak. A request has a method, path, and headers (and maybe a body); a response has a status code, headers, and a body. Methods express intent, status codes report the outcome, and headers carry metadata like content type, caching rules, auth, and CORS permissions. HTTPS wraps it in TLS encryption.
foundations.formalDefinition: HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol over TCP; HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. Requests carry a method + path + headers (+ optional body); responses carry a status code + headers + body.
foundations.whyItMatters: You call APIs, cache responses, handle auth, and debug failures through HTTP. Knowing status codes and headers is the difference between fixing a 401 vs a 403 vs a CORS error correctly.
foundations.mentalModel: A postcard exchange: the method is what you're asking for, the status code is the reply stamp (delivered/moved/refused), and headers are the notes in the margins.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser sets many headers automatically (Origin, Cookie, Accept) and enforces rules like CORS based on response headers.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Designing/consuming REST endpoints, setting Cache-Control, handling 401/403 auth flows, and diagnosing failed fetches.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct status codes and caching headers improve reliability, cacheability, and client behavior across the product.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Reading status codes and headers lets you fix the actual failure layer instead of guessing.
foundations.performanceImpact: Cache-Control, ETags, and compression headers cut bytes and round-trips; keep-alive and HTTP/2 reduce connection overhead.
commonUseCases: Consuming a REST API with fetch

commonMisconceptions.reality: 401 = not authenticated (who are you?); 403 = authenticated but not allowed (you can't do this).

commonMisconceptions.myth: A CORS error is a server being down.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's the browser blocking a cross-origin response that lacks the right Access-Control-* headers; the request often succeeded server-side.

theory.question: What's the difference between 401 and 403, and what is a CORS error really?
theory.directAnswer: 401 Unauthorized means you're not authenticated — the server doesn't know who you are (missing/invalid credentials). 403 Forbidden means you're authenticated but not allowed to do this. A CORS error is different: the request usually reached the server, but the browser blocks the response from being read by JS because the response lacked the required Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and related) headers for your origin.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: HTTP outcome semantics and the browser's cross-origin security model.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Precise status semantics and CORS are constant sources of confusion and interview questions.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Servers pick status codes; browsers enforce CORS based on response headers and the request's Origin.

theory.whyImportant: Misreading these wastes hours debugging the wrong layer.

nestedTopics.title: Preflight requests
nestedTopics.explanation: For non-simple requests the browser sends an OPTIONS preflight; the server must approve method/headers.

followUps.question: How do you fix a CORS error?
followUps.answer: On the server: return Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and allow the method/headers, handling the OPTIONS preflight). It's a server-config fix, not a client one.

keyTakeaways: Methods express intent; GET is safe/idempotent, POST is not.
Status codes: 2xx ok, 3xx redirect, 4xx client, 5xx server.
Headers drive content type, caching, auth, and CORS.
HTTPS (TLS) is required for many modern browser APIs.
